sections.title: Level 2 Strategy
sections.content: In Sentence Improvement Level 2, both sentence structure and meaning must be considered. Follow 3–4 steps: Step 1: Identify the main clause and subordinate clause. Step 2: Check grammar rules such as Conditional sentences, Parallelism, and Adverb position. Step 3: Examine phrasal verbs or idiomatic usage. Step 4: Choose the correct option based on meaning and fluency.

sections.title: Improving Conditional Sentences
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the If-clause. Step 2: Determine whether it is Type 1, Type 2, or Type 3 conditional. Step 3: Match the correct tenses. Step 4: Check whether the meaning is logical. Example: 'If I would know the answer, I would tell you' is incorrect. Correct: 'If I knew the answer, I would tell you.'

sections.title: Parallelism (Parallel Structure)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify lists or conjunctions (and, or, but). Step 2: Check whether all words are in the same grammatical form. Step 3: Maintain the same structure. Step 4: Ensure clarity in the sentence. Example: 'She likes reading, to swim, and dancing' is incorrect. Correct: 'She likes reading, swimming, and dancing.'

sections.title: Correct Use of Phrasal Verbs
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the verb and particle. Step 2: Understand the correct meaning of the phrasal verb. Step 3: Match it with the sentence context. Step 4: Select the correct option. Example: 'He gave in smoking' is incorrect. Correct: 'He gave up smoking.'

sections.title: Correct Placement of Adverbs
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the adverb (only, even, enough). Step 2: Check which word it modifies. Step 3: Place it near that word. Step 4: Ensure clarity of meaning. Example: 'She only said that she was tired' may change meaning depending on placement. Correct placement: 'She said that she was only tired.'

sections.title: Correction in Question Tags
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the subject and verb of the main clause. Step 2: Use a negative tag with a positive clause and a positive tag with a negative clause. Step 3: Choose the correct auxiliary verb. Step 4: Match the pronoun subject correctly. Example: 'She is coming, isn't she?'

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Conditional tense mismatch. 2. Using different grammatical forms in a list. 3. Choosing the wrong phrasal verb. 4. Placing adverbs incorrectly. 5. Using the wrong auxiliary in question tags.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 2, sentence structure and context are important. Match tenses correctly in conditionals, maintain the same form in parallelism, understand the meaning of phrasal verbs, place adverbs correctly, and ensure subject–verb balance in question tags.

tricks.title: Type 2 Conditional Identification
tricks.explanation: If + past tense, main clause uses would + verb.
tricks.example: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.

tricks.title: Type 3 Conditional Identification
tricks.explanation: If + had + past participle, main clause uses would have + past participle.
tricks.example: If she had studied, she would have passed.

tricks.title: Parallel Form Shortcut
tricks.explanation: After And/Or, keep the form of all items the same.
tricks.example: He enjoys reading, writing, and painting.

tricks.title: Remember Common Phrasal Verbs
tricks.explanation: Give up = stop, Give in = surrender.
tricks.example: He gave up smoking last year.

tricks.title: Only Placement Rule
tricks.explanation: Place 'only' close to the word it modifies.

tricks.title: Enough Placement Rule
tricks.explanation: Enough usually comes after an adjective or adverb.
tricks.example: He is old enough to drive.

tricks.title: Positive Clause = Negative Tag
tricks.explanation: If the sentence is positive, the tag should be negative.

tricks.title: Negative Clause = Positive Tag
tricks.explanation: If the sentence is negative, the tag should be positive.

tricks.title: Auxiliary Match Trick
tricks.explanation: Use the same auxiliary verb in the question tag as in the main clause.
